name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q01 - Membrane transport mechanisms and characteristics

questiontext.text:
Match the transport processes with their correct descriptions.

Transport ProcessDescription
(A) Simple diffusion(i) Uses ATP to pump molecules uphill against a concentration gradient
(B) Facilitated diffusion(ii) Passive movement down a gradient without special membrane proteins
(C) Active transport(iii) Single molecule crosses membrane independently via a carrier protein
(D) Uniport(iv) Passive movement down a gradient requiring special membrane proteins

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transport across biological membranes is classified based on energy expenditure, involvement of membrane proteins, and direction relative to the concentration gradient.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Concept
- Simple diffusion is a passive process occurring down a concentration gradient without requiring special membrane proteins or ATP.
- Facilitated diffusion is also passive and occurs only along a pre-existing concentration gradient without ATP expenditure, but it requires special membrane proteins.
- Active transport uses ATP energy to pump substances uphill (from low to high concentration) against a concentration gradient.
- Uniport occurs when a carrier protein transports a single type of molecule across the membrane independently of other molecules.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each process to its description gives: Simple diffusion — passive movement without membrane proteins; Facilitated diffusion — passive movement requiring membrane proteins; Active transport — ATP-driven uphill transport; Uniport — independent movement of a single molecule. Thus, the correct pairing is A–ii, B–iv, C–i, D–iii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q02 - Porins, aquaporins, symport, and antiport

questiontext.text:
Match the membrane transport structures/modes with their correct features.

Structure / ModeFeature
(A) Porins(i) Two types of molecules cross the membrane in opposite directions
(B) Aquaporins(ii) Eight different types of proteins forming water channels
(C) Symport(iii) Proteins forming large pores in outer membranes of plastids and mitochondria
(D) Antiport(iv) Two types of molecules cross the membrane in the same direction

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Facilitated diffusion relies on specialised channel and carrier proteins in biological membranes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Concept
- Porins are proteins that form large pores in the outer membranes of plastids, mitochondria, and some bacteria, allowing molecules up to the size of small proteins to pass through.
- Aquaporins are water channels made up of eight different types of proteins.
- In a symport, two types of molecules move together across the membrane in the same direction.
- In an antiport, two types of molecules move simultaneously across the membrane in opposite directions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is A–iii, B–ii, C–iv, D–i.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q03 - Plant cell responses to external solutions

questiontext.text:
Match the external condition or system with the corresponding state of the plant cell or water potential.

Condition / SystemResulting State / Value
(A) Hypotonic external solution(i) Cell becomes flaccid with no net flow of water
(B) Hypertonic external solution(ii) Water potential is zero by convention
(C) Isotonic external solution(iii) Cell swells and builds turgor pressure
(D) Pure water at atmospheric pressure(iv) Protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The osmotic behaviour of a plant cell depends on the water potential difference between its cytoplasm and the surrounding external solution.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Concept
- In a hypotonic solution (more dilute than the cytoplasm), water diffuses into the cell, causing it to swell and build up turgor pressure against the rigid cell wall.
- In a hypertonic solution (more concentrated than the cytoplasm), water moves out of the cell, causing the protoplast to shrink away from the cell wall (plasmolysis).
- In an isotonic solution, the external solution balances the osmotic pressure of the cytoplasm, resulting in no net flow of water and a flaccid cell.
- Pure water at standard temperatures and atmospheric pressure has the maximum water potential, taken as zero by convention.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct pairing is A–iii, B–iv, C–i, D–ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q04 - Water potential components, osmotic pressure, and imbibition

questiontext.text:
Match the plant-water relation terms with their correct definitions or characteristics.

TermCharacteristic
(A) Solute potential (\(\Psi_s\))(i) Positive pressure applied to prevent water from diffusing in
(B) Pressure potential (\(\Psi_p\))(ii) Absorption of water by solid colloids such as dry seeds and wood
(C) Osmotic pressure(iii) Always negative due to lowering of free energy by dissolved solutes
(D) Imbibition(iv) Usually positive in turgid cells, though negative tension occurs in xylem

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water movement in plant cells is governed by solute potential, pressure potential, osmotic pressure, and special diffusive processes like imbibition.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Concept
- Solute potential (\(\Psi_s\)) represents the lowering of water potential due to dissolution of solutes and is always negative.
- Pressure potential (\(\Psi_p\)) is usually positive in turgid cells, though negative potential (tension) in the xylem water column plays a major role in upward transport.
- Osmotic pressure is the positive external pressure required to prevent water from diffusing across a selectively permeable membrane; it is numerically equal to osmotic potential but opposite in sign.
- Imbibition is a special type of diffusion in which water is absorbed by solids (colloids) such as dry seeds and wood, causing them to swell.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is A–iii, B–iv, C–i, D–ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q05 - Root water absorption pathways and mycorrhiza

questiontext.text:
Match the root absorption pathways and associated structures with their correct descriptions.

Pathway / StructureDescription
(A) Apoplast pathway(i) Symbiotic association of a fungus with a root system
(B) Symplast pathway(ii) Impervious band of suberised matrix in the endodermis
(C) Casparian strip(iii) Water movement through interconnected protoplasts via plasmodesmata
(D) Mycorrhiza(iv) Water movement through adjacent cell walls and intercellular spaces

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water absorbed by root hairs moves inward through root tissues via two distinct pathways and may be assisted by symbiotic fungal associations.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Concept
- The apoplast pathway occurs exclusively through intercellular spaces and adjacent cell walls without crossing cell membranes.
- The symplast pathway involves water moving through interconnected protoplasts via cytoplasmic strands extending through plasmodesmata.
- The Casparian strip is a suberised, water-impervious band in the endodermis that blocks apoplastic flow.
- A mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association between fungal hyphae and a plant root system, aiding in mineral and water absorption.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matching is A–iv, B–iii, C–ii, D–i.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q06 - Physical properties of water and guttation

questiontext.text:
Match the properties or phenomena related to xylem water transport with their correct explanations.

Property / PhenomenonExplanation
(A) Cohesion(i) Loss of water in liquid phase from vein endings near leaf tips
(B) Adhesion(ii) Mutual attraction between water molecules
(C) Surface tension(iii) Greater attraction of water molecules to each other in liquid phase than gas phase
(D) Guttation(iv) Attraction of water molecules to polar surfaces of tracheary elements

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The transpiration-driven ascent of xylem sap depends on specific physical properties of water, while root pressure can cause liquid exudation when evaporation is low.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Concept
- Cohesion is the mutual attraction between water molecules.
- Adhesion is the attraction of water molecules to polar surfaces, such as the walls of tracheary elements (tracheids and vessel elements).
- Surface tension arises because water molecules are attracted to each other more strongly in the liquid phase than to water in the gas phase.
- Guttation is the loss of excess water in its liquid phase around special vein openings near the tips of grass blades and herbaceous leaves during night and early morning.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct pairing is A–ii, B–iv, C–iii, D–i.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q07 - Stomatal structure, leaf distribution, and C4 efficiency

questiontext.text:
Match the anatomical or physiological features related to transpiration with their correct characteristics.

FeatureCharacteristic
(A) Inner wall of guard cell(i) Radially oriented to make stomatal opening easier
(B) Cellulose microfibrils of guard cell(ii) Loses half as much water as a \(\text{C}_3\) plant per \(\text{CO}_2\) fixed
(C) Dorsiventral leaf(iii) Thick and elastic towards the stomatal aperture
(D) \(\text{C}_4\) plant(iv) Greater number of stomata on the lower surface

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Stomatal mechanics depend on guard cell wall structure, stomatal distribution varies with leaf anatomy, and photosynthetic pathways balance carbon fixation against water loss.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Concept
- The inner wall of each guard cell facing the stomatal aperture is thick and elastic, curving into a crescent shape when turgid.
- Cellulose microfibrils in guard cell walls are oriented radially rather than longitudinally, facilitating stomatal opening.
- In a dorsiventral (dicotyledonous) leaf, the lower surface usually has a greater number of stomata.
- A \(\text{C}_4\) plant is twice as efficient as a \(\text{C}_3\) plant at fixing \(\text{CO}_2\) and loses only half as much water for the same amount of \(\text{CO}_2\) fixed.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is A–iii, B–i, C–iv, D–ii.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q08 - Mineral ion uptake, endodermal control, and remobilisation

questiontext.text:
Match the structures or mineral elements with their correct physiological roles in nutrient uptake and remobilisation.

Structure / ElementPhysiological Role
(A) Root hair epidermal cells(i) Readily remobilised from older, senescing leaves to younger leaves
(B) Endodermal transport proteins(ii) Control points adjusting quantity and types of solutes reaching xylem
(C) Calcium(iii) Structural component that is not remobilised
(D) Phosphorus and Nitrogen(iv) Active ion uptake partly creating water potential gradient in roots

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mineral ions are absorbed selectively by root cells, regulated at the endodermis, and differentially remobilised during senescence.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Concept
- Specific proteins in root hair epidermal cells actively pump ions from the soil into the cytoplasm, partly establishing the water potential gradient for osmotic water uptake.
- Transport proteins of endodermal cells act as control points where the plant adjusts the quantity and types of solutes that reach the xylem (unidirectionally due to the suberin layer).
- Calcium is a structural component of the cell and is not remobilised from older parts.
- Phosphorus, sulphur, nitrogen, and potassium are among the elements most readily remobilised from senescing leaves to growing regions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct matching is A–iv, B–ii, C–iii, D–i.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_TRANSPORTINPLANTS_Q09 - Phloem translocation, sieve plates, and girdling

questiontext.text:
Match the features of phloem transport with their correct descriptions.

Phloem FeatureDescription
(A) Primary sugar translocated(i) Demonstrates phloem is responsible for downward food translocation
(B) Direction of phloem flow(ii) Perforated end walls of sieve tube cells forming continuous filaments
(C) Sieve plates(iii) Bi-directional due to variable source–sink relationship
(D) Girdling experiment(iv) Sucrose, a disaccharide

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phloem translocates organic food from variable sources to sinks via specialised living sieve tube columns.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Concept
- Glucose synthesised at the source is converted to sucrose (a disaccharide), which is the primary form of sugar translocated in phloem sap.
- Because the source–sink relationship varies with season and plant needs, phloem transport is bi-directional (upward or downward).
- Sieve tube cells form long columns with holes in their end walls called sieve plates, through which cytoplasmic strands pass.
- The girdling experiment (removing a ring of bark up to the phloem layer) causes swelling above the ring, demonstrating that phloem translocates food downward toward the roots.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct matching is A–iv, B–iii, C–ii, D–i.
